meta.description: Widely credited to Marie Curie, but no letter, book or speech of hers with this line has been found. Wikiquote cites only a 2006 trading almanac.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are sadistic scientists who hurry to hunt down errors instead of establishing the truth'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Marie Curie everywhere, sourced nowhere: no Curie text with this line has been found. Wikiquote's only citation is a 2006 almanac.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Curie, and the jab fits the scientific feuds of her day. But no letter, book, lecture or interview of hers containing this wording has been located. Wikiquote’s only citation is The Commodity Trader’s Almanac 2007 (2006), and the line does not appear in her own memoir Pierre Curie (1923).

source.heading: Where the line can be traced

docMeta.dd: Pierre Curie (1923, Kellogg trans.); Eve Curie, Madame Curie (1938 English ed., Sheean trans.)

source.excerpt: There are sadistic scientists who hurry to hunt down errors instead of establishing the truth.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its Quotes section, but its only citation is a secondary one: “As quoted in The Commodity Trader’s Almanac 2007 (2006) by Scott W. Barrie and Jeffrey A. Hirsch, p. 44.”

We searched the full text of Curie’s own Pierre Curie (Macmillan, 1923; trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg) ↗, which includes her autobiographical notes. It contains no “sadistic,” “hunt down” or “establishing the truth.”
We also searched the full text of the 1938 English edition of Eve Curie’s biography of her mother, Madame Curie, translated by Vincent Sheean ↗. The word “sadistic” does not appear in it.
By 2011 it was circulating unsourced in popular science media: a Gizmodo listicle of 6 May 2011 ↗ presented it as Curie “verbally slapping” other scientists, citing only general quote sites.
source.excerptNote: This is the popular wording. Curie wrote mainly in French and Polish, and no original-language text for this line has been found, so it is unknown whether the English is a translation or a modern paraphrase.
source.rightsNote: Because no work by Curie containing this wording has been found, its first publication and translator are unknown, so no copyright status is asserted. Curie’s own Pierre Curie (1923) is public domain in the US, but the line is not in it.

author.name: Marie Curie
author.heading: About the person it's credited to
author.bio: Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Curie did her life’s work in Paris, where she pioneered the study of radioactivity and discovered polonium and radium. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and she is still the only person to have won Nobels in two sciences: physics (1903) and chemistry (1911).

misattribution.heading: How the line travels
misattribution.intro: The line usually reaches readers with Curie’s name and no source attached. The places it is easiest to find all repeat it rather than document it.

items.why: They print the exact popular wording under Curie’s name. Quotewise ↗ shows no book, letter or date for it.
The listicle ↗ frames the line as Curie getting the last word in a scientific feud, but its only sources are general quotation websites.
Wikiquote ↗ places it among Curie’s quotes but cites a 2006 commodity-trading almanac, not anything Curie wrote or said.

misattribution.truthLine: No text by Marie Curie containing this sentence has been located. It is not in her memoir Pierre Curie ↗, so treat it as an attribution, not a documented quotation.

context.heading: Why the attribution is hard to settle
lead: The sentence reads like a complaint about critics who look for flaws instead of doing their own work, and Curie did face harsh public and scientific attacks. But a line that fits someone’s life is not evidence that she said it. Curie wrote mainly in French and Polish, and no original-language version of this sentence has been traced.
Without that original, nobody can say whether the English wording is a translation of something she wrote, a paraphrase, or a line attached to her later.
context.detailsSummary: What we checked, and what we could not
detailsBody: We searched the full texts of Curie’s own Pierre Curie (1923) ↗ and of the 1938 English edition of Eve Curie’s Madame Curie ↗. Neither contains the line.

A slightly different wording, “hasten to hunt down error,” has been reported in Alan L. Mackay’s 1977 anthology The Harvest of a Quiet Eye: A Selection of Scientific Quotations ↗. That book is available only as a lending copy and we could not open it, so we have not confirmed the entry, its wording, or any source it gives. Quote Investigator has not published an investigation of this quote.
context.pull: Fits her life, but no document of hers has turned up.
